2518: Most scholars attribute the core oracles to Amos in the mid 8th century BC. Several passages are widely debated as later additions, especially the oracle against Judah (Amos 2:4-5), the hymn fragments (e.g. Amos 4:13; Amos 5:8-9) and the hopeful ending (Amos 9:11-15), which many date to the exile; others argue they fit Amos' own message, since judgment and hope are paired in many prophets.
2520: The prosperous northern kingdom of Israel, especially its wealthy elite and the royal sanctuary at Bethel.
2521: The reign of Jeroboam II of Israel and Uzziah of Judah, 'two years before the earthquake' (Amos 1:1), a period of expansion, wealth and complacency.
2522: To confront Israel's social injustice, exploitation of the poor and hollow worship, to announce that the Day of the LORD will be darkness for them, and to call for justice to roll down like waters.
2523: Social justice and care for the poor
2527: The Day of the LORD as judgment
2529: Oracles against the nations, climaxing with Israel
2532: Cows of Bashan; 'yet you did not return'
2533: Seek the LORD and live; let justice roll down
2534: Woe to those at ease in Zion
2538: Basket of summer fruit; famine of the word
2540: Amos insists that God's covenant people are held to his standard of justice and that religious privilege offers no protection from judgment. At the Jerusalem council James cites Amos 9:11-12 to show that the inclusion of Gentiles fulfils the promised rebuilding of David's tent (Acts 15:15-17).
2541: Third book of the Twelve in the Hebrew order; second in the Septuagint. The Septuagint of Amos 9:11-12 differs from the Hebrew ('the rest of men may seek the Lord' rather than 'possess the remnant of Edom'); Acts 15 follows the Greek.
2544: Obadiah ('servant of the LORD'), otherwise unknown. Some Jewish tradition identified him with Ahab's steward Obadiah (1 Kgs 18:3), though most traditional scholars do not accept this.
2545: Anonymous beyond the name. Because it closely parallels Jer 49:7-22 and seems to describe Edom's gloating at Jerusalem's fall (compare Ps 137:7), most scholars date it shortly after 586 BC. A minority of conservative scholars link it to an earlier Edomite revolt and raid in the reign of Jehoram (2 Kgs 8:20-22), c. 845 BC.
2546: Early date under Jehoram of Judah
2547: Judah, grieving the destruction of Jerusalem and the betrayal of Edom, their 'brother' nation descended from Esau.
2548: The aftermath of an attack on Jerusalem in which Edom looted the city and handed over refugees, most likely the Babylonian conquest of 586 BC.
2549: To announce God's judgment on Edom's pride and violence against Judah, and to promise that on the Day of the LORD Zion will be restored and 'the kingdom shall be the LORD's'.
2552: As you have done, it will be done to you
2553: The Day of the LORD for all nations
2554: The kingdom belongs to the LORD
2556: Edom's violence against his brother Jacob
2557: The Day of the LORD and Zion's restoration
2558: Obadiah continues the long story of Jacob and Esau that began in Genesis, showing that hostility to God's people will not have the last word. Its closing note that 'the kingdom shall be the LORD's' points toward the universal reign of God proclaimed in the Gospels and Revelation (Rev 11:15).
2559: Fourth book of the Twelve in the Hebrew order and the shortest book of the Old Testament (21 verses). Its relation to Jer 49:7-22 suggests either borrowing in one direction or a shared earlier oracle.
2561: Narrative about a prophet (historical narrative or didactic story, debated) with a psalm
2562: Jonah son of Amittai, a prophet from Gath-hepher in the reign of Jeroboam II (2 Kgs 14:25), or someone writing soon after about him. Jesus speaks of Jonah's sign and of Nineveh's repentance alongside historical figures such as the queen of the south (Matt 12:39-42), which many take as treating the story as historical.
2563: The book is written about Jonah in the third person, by an anonymous author. Many critical scholars date it to the Persian period, citing late linguistic features and its theme of God's mercy to foreigners, and read it as a didactic story, parable or satire rather than history; others hold that it reflects a real prophet's experience. Some regard the psalm in Jonah 2 as an earlier composition inserted into the narrative.
2564: Israelites who resented God's mercy to their enemies and assumed his favour belonged to them alone.
2565: Joppa, the Mediterranean Sea and the great Assyrian city of Nineveh in the 8th century BC, before Assyria destroyed Israel.
2566: To show the sovereign mercy of God toward all peoples, even Israel's worst enemies, to expose the prophet's (and readers') narrow resentment, and to end with God's open question about compassion.
2572: Jonah flees; storm and the great fish
2576: Jonah reminds Israel that the God who chose Abraham meant to bless all nations, a purpose fulfilled when the gospel goes to the Gentiles. Jesus calls his own death and resurrection 'the sign of the prophet Jonah' (Matt 12:39-41).
2577: Fifth book of the Twelve in the Hebrew order; sixth in the Septuagint. It is read in the synagogue on the afternoon of Yom Kippur as a lesson in repentance. Hebrew Bibles number English Jonah 1:17 as 2:1, so Jonah 2 has eleven verses in Hebrew.
2580: Micah of Moresheth, a town in the Judean lowlands, who prophesied in the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (Mic 1:1). A century later the elders of Judah quoted his warning against Jerusalem (Jer 26:18).
2581: There is broad agreement that most of Mic 1-3 comes from Micah in the late 8th century BC. The hopeful oracles in Mic 4-5 and the material in Mic 6-7 are debated: many scholars regard parts as exilic or post-exilic additions, others as Micah's own words or from his circle. Mic 4:1-3 is nearly identical to Isa 2:2-4, and scholars debate which is the source or whether both draw on a common oracle.
2582: Final edition with exilic and post-exilic additions
2583: Judah and Jerusalem, and also Samaria, in the late 8th century, especially corrupt rulers, priests and prophets who exploited the poor.
2584: The era of Assyrian expansion: the fall of Samaria (722 BC) and Sennacherib's invasion of Judah (701 BC), which devastated Micah's own lowland region.
2585: To announce judgment on both Samaria and Jerusalem for injustice and false religion, to promise a remnant and a ruler from Bethlehem who will shepherd God's people, and to summarise what the LORD requires.
2586: Justice for the poor and judgment on corrupt leaders
2589: Nations streaming to Zion in peace
2590: Do justly, love mercy, walk humbly
2591: God who pardons and delights in mercy
2593: The LORD comes against Samaria and Judah
2594: Woe to those who seize fields
2595: Corrupt rulers and prophets; Zion ploughed
2601: Micah holds together God's judgment on injustice and his promise of a Davidic shepherd who will bring peace to the ends of the earth. The chief priests and scribes cite Mic 5:2 to tell Herod where the Messiah would be born (Matt 2:5-6), and Mic 7:20 recalls God's oath to Abraham and Jacob.
2602: Sixth book of the Twelve in the Hebrew order; third in the Septuagint. Hebrew Bibles number English Mic 5:1 as 4:14, so English Mic 5:2 is Hebrew 5:1.
2604: Prophecy (oracle against a nation, vivid poetry)
2605: Nahum the Elkoshite (Nah 1:1); the location of Elkosh is unknown.
2606: Generally accepted as the work of a 7th-century Judean prophet. Nah 1 contains a partial alphabetic acrostic hymn, which some regard as an independent psalm adapted as an introduction. The reference to the fall of Thebes (No-Amon) to Assyria in 663 BC (Nah 3:8) and the anticipation of Nineveh's fall in 612 BC set the window of composition.
2607: Shortly after the fall of Thebes
2609: Judah, long oppressed by Assyria, assured that the cruel empire would fall.
2610: Judah under Assyrian domination, between 663 and 612 BC, when Nineveh was destroyed by the Babylonians and Medes.
2611: To proclaim that the LORD, though slow to anger, will not leave the guilty unpunished, and that Nineveh's violent empire will be destroyed, bringing good news of peace to Judah.
2613: The LORD is slow to anger yet great in power
2614: Refuge for those who trust him
2615: The end of the bloody city
2617: The LORD's character: avenger and refuge
2620: Nahum is a sequel to Jonah: the same Nineveh that once repented has returned to violence, and God's patience gives way to judgment. Its announcement of the herald 'that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace' (Nah 1:15) parallels Isa 52:7, which Paul applies to gospel preachers (Rom 10:15).
2621: Seventh book of the Twelve. Hebrew Bibles number English Nah 1:15 as 2:1.
2623: Prophecy (dialogue with God, woe oracles and a psalm)
2624: Habakkuk the prophet (Hab 1:1; Hab 3:1), about whom the book says nothing more. A later legend in the Greek additions to Daniel (Bel and the Dragon) has him carry food to Daniel in the lions' den.
2625: Generally attributed to a Judean prophet of the late 7th century BC. Some scholars think the psalm in Hab 3, with its musical notations, circulated separately; the Qumran commentary (Pesher Habakkuk, 1QpHab) covers only Hab 1-2, though this may reflect the commentator's purpose rather than a shorter book.
2628: Faithful Judeans troubled by injustice at home and by God's use of the brutal Babylonians to punish it.
2629: Judah in the reign of Jehoiakim, as the Chaldeans (Babylonians) rose to dominance after the battle of Carchemish (605 BC).
2630: To wrestle honestly with God over evil and injustice, to receive the answer that the righteous shall live by faith(fulness) while the proud oppressor will fall, and to model trust and joy in God even amid loss.
2632: The righteous shall live by faith
2634: The earth filled with the knowledge of God's glory
2635: Joy in God when everything fails
2636: First complaint and God's answer: the Chaldeans
2637: Second complaint: how can the holy God use the wicked?
2638: God's answer: the vision and five woes
2639: The just shall live by faith
2641: Habakkuk's prayer and song of trust
2642: Habakkuk shows faith learning to wait for God's justice through the coming catastrophe of exile. Its statement that 'the just shall live by his faith' (Hab 2:4) is quoted three times in the New Testament (Rom 1:17; Gal 3:11; Heb 10:38) and became central to Paul's teaching and to the Reformation.
2643: Eighth book of the Twelve. The Septuagint of Hab 2:4 reads 'the righteous shall live by my faith(fulness)', and Heb 10:37-38 follows a form of the Greek.
2646: Zephaniah, whose genealogy is traced back four generations to a Hezekiah (Zeph 1:1), often taken to be King Hezekiah, which would make the prophet a member of the royal family.
2647: Most scholars accept a core from Zephaniah in Josiah's reign, probably before the reform of 622 BC since idolatrous practices are still openly condemned. The hopeful passages in Zeph 3:9-20 are attributed by some to exilic or post-exilic editors and defended by others as integral.
2650: Judah and Jerusalem under King Josiah, including officials, priests and those mixing worship of the LORD with Baal and astral gods.
2651: Jerusalem during the reign of Josiah (640–609 BC), as Assyrian power declined.
2652: To warn of the great and terrible Day of the LORD against Judah and the nations, to urge the humble to seek the LORD, and to promise a purified remnant over whom God will rejoice with singing.
2657: The Day of the LORD against Judah
2661: Purified lips and a humble remnant
2662: Song of joy: the LORD in your midst
2663: Zephaniah gathers the prophetic theme of the Day of the LORD into a single sweeping vision of judgment followed by a joyful restored people. Its description of that day as a 'day of wrath' (Zeph 1:15) inspired the medieval hymn *Dies Irae*, and its picture of the LORD as king in Zion's midst anticipates the gospel's announcement of God dwelling with his people.
2664: Ninth book of the Twelve and the last of the pre-exilic prophets in its order; Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi follow from the post-exilic period.
2666: Prophecy (dated prophetic sermons with brief narrative)
2667: Haggai the prophet, active with Zechariah in encouraging the rebuilding of the temple (Ezra 5:1; Ezra 6:14).
2668: The messages are widely accepted as Haggai's, but they are reported in the third person, so many scholars think a close associate or editor arranged them soon afterward, perhaps together with Zech 1-8 as a combined work on the temple's rebuilding.
2669: Zerubbabel the governor, Joshua the high priest and the returned exiles in Jerusalem, who had let the temple lie in ruins while building their own houses.
2670: Jerusalem in the second year of Darius I of Persia, between August and December 520 BC, about eighteen years after the first return.
2671: To rouse the community to rebuild the temple, to explain their economic hardship as the result of misplaced priorities, and to promise that God's glory would fill the house and that Zerubbabel would be his chosen signet ring.
2672: Consider your ways: priorities and God's house
2674: The latter glory greater than the former
2677: Call to rebuild and the people's response
2678: The glory of the latter house
2679: From this day I will bless you
2681: Haggai marks the rebuilding of the second temple and keeps alive the hope attached to David's line through Zerubbabel, who appears in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:12-13). Hebrews quotes Hag 2:6 about God shaking heaven and earth to point to an unshakable kingdom (Heb 12:26-28).
2682: Tenth book of the Twelve; along with Zechariah and Malachi it belongs to the post-exilic prophets.
2684: Prophecy (night visions, sermons and apocalyptic-style oracles)
2685: Zechariah son of Berechiah, son of Iddo (Zech 1:1), a priest-prophet who returned from exile and worked alongside Haggai (Ezra 5:1). Defenders of unity point to shared themes across the book, such as the cleansing of Jerusalem, the shepherd and the coming king.
2686: Most scholars distinguish Zech 1-8 (dated to 520–518 BC, from Zechariah himself) from Zech 9-14 (often called Deutero-Zechariah, with no dates, a different style and a looser historical setting), which many place in the 5th century or later, perhaps the early Greek period given the mention of Greece (Zech 9:13). Some further divide Zech 9-11 and Zech 12-14, each introduced by 'the burden of the word of the LORD'.
2689: The returned exiles in Jerusalem and their leaders Zerubbabel and Joshua, discouraged by small beginnings and foreign domination.
2690: Jerusalem during the rebuilding of the temple under Darius I (from 520 BC), with later oracles looking toward future conflicts and the final day of the LORD.
2691: To call the people to return to the LORD, to encourage temple rebuilding through visions of God's renewed care for Jerusalem, and to announce a coming humble king, a rejected shepherd and the final day when the LORD will be king over all the earth.
2692: Return to me and I will return to you
2693: Not by might, but by my Spirit
2694: Cleansing of the priesthood and the land
2696: The pierced one and the struck shepherd
2697: The LORD king over all the earth
2703: Flying scroll, woman in a basket, four chariots
2705: Questions about fasting; promises to Zion
2706: First burden: the coming king and the shepherds
2707: Your king comes on a donkey
2708: The rejected shepherd and thirty pieces of silver
2709: Second burden: the day of the LORD
2711: A fountain for cleansing; the shepherd struck
2712: Zechariah keeps the hope of a coming king and a cleansed people alive in the modest days after the exile. The Gospels draw on it heavily in the passion story: Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey (Matt 21:4-5), is betrayed for thirty pieces of silver (Matt 27:9-10), is the struck shepherd whose sheep scatter (Matt 26:31) and the pierced one on whom people look (John 19:37).
2713: Eleventh book of the Twelve and the longest of them. Matt 27:9-10 attributes a passage drawing on Zech 11:12-13 to Jeremiah, probably because it combines Zechariah with themes from Jeremiah (e.g. Jer 32:6-9).
2716: A prophet named Malachi (Mal 1:1). Some ancient Jewish tradition (the Targum and the Talmud, Megillah 15a, in one opinion) identified him with Ezra, since 'Malachi' means 'my messenger'.
2717: Because *mal'akhi* means 'my messenger' and echoes Mal 3:1, many scholars think it is a title rather than a personal name, making the book anonymous; the heading 'the burden of the word of the LORD' matches Zech 9:1 and Zech 12:1, suggesting the three were once collected together. The content is generally dated to the mid 5th century BC, after the second temple was rebuilt and before or around the reforms of Ezra and Nehemiah.
2719: Earlier, soon after the temple's completion
2720: The post-exilic community in Judah, especially priests offering blemished sacrifices and people grown cynical about God's love and justice.
2721: Jerusalem under Persian rule, with a functioning temple and a governor (Mal 1:8), but with lax worship, broken marriages and neglected tithes.
2722: To answer the people's cynical questions, to rebuke careless priests and covenant-breaking, to call for wholehearted worship, and to promise the coming of the LORD's messenger and of Elijah before the great day of the LORD.
2723: God's covenant love questioned and affirmed
2724: Honour due to God in worship
2726: The messenger who prepares the way
2727: The day of the LORD and the sun of righteousness
2728: Remember the law of Moses; Elijah will come
2732: The messenger of the covenant and refining judgment
2733: Return to me: robbing God in tithes
2734: The book of remembrance and the coming day
2736: In Christian Bibles Malachi closes the Old Testament with a promise of the messenger and of Elijah, and the Gospels open by announcing that John the Baptist is that forerunner (Mark 1:2; Matt 11:10-14; Luke 1:17). Its call to remember Moses and wait for Elijah ties Law and Prophets together, as they appear again with Jesus at the transfiguration (Matt 17:3).
2737: Last of the Twelve and the last book of the Protestant Old Testament; the Hebrew Bible instead ends with Chronicles, and Hebrew Bibles number English Mal 4:1-6 as Mal 3:19-24. The Latin Vulgate and older Catholic Bibles such as the Douay-Rheims place the deuterocanonical *1 and 2 Maccabees* after Malachi, at the end of the Old Testament (modern Catholic Bibles such as the NAB place them after Esther). They recount the Jewish revolt against Antiochus IV Epiphanes (167–164 BC) and the rededication of the temple remembered at Hanukkah. Orthodox Bibles also include *3 Maccabees*, with *4 Maccabees* in an appendix; Protestant Bibles that print 1–2 Maccabees place them among the Apocrypha.
